source: CARDI (Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute) technical bulletin, "Selecting Rice Varieties for Rainfed Lowland Cultivation" (ការជ្រើសរើសពូជស្រូវសម្រាប់ការដាំដុះតំបន់ទំនាបរំពឹងទឹកភ្លៀង), CARDI, funded through the Cambodia-Australia Agricultural Extension Project (CAAEP/AusAID)
text:
When choosing which rice variety to grow, CARDI recommends farmers weigh three main priorities: (1) pick a variety that genuinely suits and responds well to the specific water/ecosystem conditions of the field (e.g. flood depth, drainage, duration of standing water); (2) pick a variety with eating and milling quality that matches what domestic and export markets actually want; and (3) pick a variety with good resistance to the diseases and insect pests common in the area.

To compare varieties consistently, CARDI's variety-description system scores several plant and grain traits on standardized scales. These scales are useful for farmers and extension workers reading a variety-description sheet or catalog entry:

PLANT HEIGHT (measured from soil surface to the top of the panicle at maturity):
- Short: under 75 cm
- Medium: 85-105 cm
- Medium-tall: 110-130 cm
- Tall: over 130 cm

LODGING RESISTANCE (percentage of plants fallen over at maturity, scored 0-9):
- 0 = no lodging
- 1 = under 20% of plants lodged
- 3 = 20-40% lodged
- 5 = 41-60% lodged
- 7 = 61-80% lodged
- 9 = over 80% lodged (very poor lodging resistance)
Lower scores mean sturdier, more lodging-resistant varieties — an important trait where wind or heavy rain at maturity is common.

THRESHING EASE / SHATTERING (how easily grain separates from the panicle when handled, scored 1-9 based on roughly how many grains come loose per hand-pull test):
- 1 = very hard to thresh (about 1 grain comes loose)
- 3 = moderately hard (1-5 grains)
- 5 = medium (6-25 grains)
- 7 = easy (26-50 grains)
- 9 = very easy/shatters readily (51-100 grains)
Varieties that are too easy to thresh risk field losses from grain shattering before harvest; varieties that are too hard to thresh increase post-harvest labor.

MILLING/GRAIN-FILL YIELD (share of the harvested rough rice that becomes usable product after milling):
- Husk (rice hull removed during milling): typically 20-22% of rough rice weight
- Bran (removed during polishing): typically 8-10%
- Net milled rice yield: typically 68-70% of the original rough rice weight
A variety with a very low net-milled-rice percentage effectively gives farmers less sellable product for the same amount of paddy harvested.

GRAIN LENGTH (measured on milled/dehusked grain, in millimeters):
- Very long: over 7.55 mm
- Long: 6.61-7.50 mm
- Medium: 5.51-6.60 mm
- Short: under 5.50 mm

GRAIN SHAPE (ratio of grain length to grain width):
- Slender: ratio over 3.0
- Medium: ratio 2.1-3.0
- Bold: ratio 1.1-2.0
- Round: ratio 1.0 or less
Market preference for grain shape varies — export markets often favor long, slender grain, while some domestic preferences differ.

AROMA AND GLUTINOUS TESTING: aroma is checked using a simple chemical test on a sample of husked grain (a KOH — potassium hydroxide — soak test, where aromatic varieties give a distinct reaction/scent when the grain is soaked and gently crushed), and glutinous (sticky) rice character is checked by chewing texture and a similar simple field test rather than requiring a laboratory.

PHOTOPERIOD SENSITIVITY: rice varieties in Cambodia fall into two broad groups — photoperiod-sensitive varieties, which can only be harvested once a year because flowering is triggered by day length (so planting timing is flexible but flowering/harvest timing is fixed to the season); and photoperiod-insensitive varieties, which flower at a fixed number of days after planting regardless of day length, and so can potentially be grown more than once a year if water is available. Photoperiod-sensitive varieties are counted purely by days from germination to harvest, and this duration can vary somewhat depending on planting date, while insensitive varieties can be planted and harvested repeatedly within a year given adequate water.
caveat: The threshing-ease, grain-fill, and lodging percentage bands are the CARDI grading-scale definitions as published, not measurements of any specific named variety — use them to interpret a variety catalog's scores, not as recommendations in themselves.
